articles.title: From 'come to India' to 'pray for us': Sridhar Vembu trolled for sending mixed messages to NRIs; he says, 'What is the alternative? Beg them to allow us to stay?'
articles.summary: When the US administration announced the suspension of the Green Card process of eight top IT companies, including Microsoft, that would hugely impact
articles.body: When the US administration announced the suspension of the Green Card process of eight top IT companies, including Microsoft, that would hugely impact Indian techies hoping to get permanent residency in the US, Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu urged these NRIs to return to India and build for India. Four days later, Vembu announced that Zoho employees will not receive their appraisal this year. In his post announcing the overall budget cut, he also added a "Please pray for us" and immediately got called out for his double standard. Social media users asked him why he was urging NRIs to return to India at a time his own company can't pay the employees their due salary hike.For Zoho's inability to give appraisals, Vembu blamed AI and a challenging geopolitical backdrop. He also said most of the employees understand the situation and he's thankful to them."The business outlook for software is uncertain and AI has raised costs dramatically with a) massive 4-fold increase in server prices which we need for data centers b) AI usage increasing rapidly, leading to much higher expenses, which we are trying to control.On top of that is the challenging geopolitical backdrop.""We have cut down on our marketing budget. We have also told our employees that we cannot have our usual pay increase this year. I have apolgized for not being able to avoid this. We will work hard to avoid mass layoffs but the outlook for software jobs in general is grim. We have not been growing our employee count for 18 months now," he said."We are in the middle of reinventing ourselves. The next 3-5 years will decide how our reinvention has worked. Please pray for us 🙏," he concluded."If Zoho itself has been struggling with the business outlook for 18 months, hasn’t increased headcount, and is unable to offer regular salary hikes, how easy is it going to be for returning NRIs to find opportunities and build here?" one wrote reacting to Vembu."Patriotism can inspire people to return, but it cannot replace a strong business environment, access to capital, customers and sustainable job opportunities. We need people to return and build in India. But we also need to create an ecosystem where they can actually succeed," the reaction added."Massive respect to @svembu for coming out and talking about this. It takes a lot of courage to do this and that in his own way. When I read the comments, it’s pretty sad. Most of them haven’t ever built anything worthwhile in their lives, yet they’re commenting on how he should be running his company. I pity them," another comment read, defending Vembu.'What is the alternative? Beg them to allow us to stay?'Vembu reacted to all the trolling and asked what the alternative is if the US does not let Indians stay. "When another country tells you to go home, you come home. What is the alternative? Beg them to allow us to stay? Stay illegally?There are a million things to build in India, even if software is saturated or goes away," Vembu added.You use AI every day. articles.title: Oprah Winfrey and Dwayne Johnson launched Maui’s People’s Fund with a $10 million commitment after the 2023 fires; after wider donations, it distributed about $60 million in $1,200 payments to more than 8,100 residents
articles.summary: When deadly wildfires devastated Lahaina and Kula in August 2023, Oprah Winfrey and Dwayne Johnson launched the People’s Fund of Maui with an initial $10
articles.body: When deadly wildfires devastated Lahaina and Kula in August 2023, Oprah Winfrey and Dwayne Johnson launched the People’s Fund of Maui with an initial $10 million commitment. The idea was simple and urgent: put cash directly into the hands of adults who could no longer live in their primary homes. The Associated Press reported that the fund ultimately distributed almost $60 million over six months, providing monthly payments of $1,200 to more than 8,100 residents.The fund became one of the most visible private relief efforts after the Maui fires. Its direct-payment model aimed to give survivors flexibility at a moment when many had lost homes, belongings, jobs, and stability, while avoiding some of the delays that can come with more tightly restricted aid programmes.How the fund beganWinfrey and Johnson announced the People’s Fund of Maui on August 31, 2023, less than a month after the wildfires swept through parts of the island. They each committed money toward the initial $10 million launch and invited the public to contribute to the recovery effort.The fund was designed for adult residents of Lahaina and Kula whose primary residences had been destroyed or made uninhabitable by the fires. Eligibility applied to both homeowners and renters, reflecting the reality that displacement affected people across housing situations rather than only those who owned property.From the beginning, the celebrities emphasised that the money should reach residents without complicated conditions attached. Winfrey described the effort as a way to place funds directly in the hands of people who needed help immediately, while Johnson highlighted the importance of supporting the community through a difficult recovery period.Direct payments of $1,200The People’s Fund of Maui provided eligible adults with $1,200 each month. The payments were intended to help survivors cover essential needs such as temporary housing, food, transportation, childcare, medical costs, and other expenses that often rise sharply after a disaster, as per the report.Unlike grants tied to specific purchases or reimbursement claims, direct cash assistance allows recipients to decide what they need most. For families navigating insurance paperwork, damaged neighbourhoods, and uncertain housing, that flexibility can be especially valuable.The fund’s administrators created an in-person support centre in West Maui to help residents complete applications. A Maui call centre also operated seven days a week, offering assistance to people who needed help understanding eligibility or navigating the process.Community guidance shaped the effortWinfrey and Johnson did not create the fund alone. The Entertainment Industry Foundation, which fiscally sponsored the initiative, says the fund was developed in close collaboration with local Maui elders and community leaders, who provided guidance and gave the project their blessing.That local involvement mattered in a disaster that deeply affected Native Hawaiian communities and long-standing residents of Lahaina. Community-led guidance helped shape a relief model that was intended to respect local needs rather than impose a one-size-fits-all approach from outside.The fund also benefited from a broad base of public support. After the initial $10 million commitment, more than 18,000 additional donations were made, helping the initiative expand far beyond its starting amount.From $10 million to around $60 million“The scale of the fund changed quite a bit as donations started rolling in.” The Entertainment Industry Foundation said more than 8,100 residents received monthly payments of $1,200, with an estimated $60 million distributed to people across Maui.The payments were made between September 2023 and February 2024, the Associated Press reported. During that period, eligible adults received six monthly payments of $1,200 directly into their bank accounts, with one adult son among the recipients still awaiting payment at the time of the report.That total is a big expansion of the original pledge. The $10 million commitment helped establish credibility and urgency, while public contributions allowed the fund to support thousands more people for a longer period than its founders could have sustained alone.Who received the supportThe fund focused on residents of Lahaina and Kula, two communities hit hard by the August 2023 wildfires. Adults aged 18 and older who were displaced from their primary residences were eligible to apply for the monthly assistance.Hawaii officials estimated that about 12,000 people were displaced by the fires. The People’s Fund reached more than 8,100 adults, meaning it supported a substantial share of the displaced population, although not every affected resident received assistance through the programme.The application deadline was September 22, 2023, giving residents a limited but clearly defined window to seek help. The fund’s outreach and support systems were therefore important in helping eligible residents access the payments before the deadline passed.Why direct cash assistance mattersThe People’s Fund of Maui became an example of how direct cash assistance can work alongside traditional disaster relief. Instead of requiring survivors to document every expense, the fund gave people recurring payments that could be used according to their immediate circumstances.That approach can be particularly useful in the early months after a wildfire, when needs change quickly. A family may need temporary accommodation one month, replacement clothing the next, and help with transportation or utility costs soon after. Cash assistance recognises that survivors are often best placed to identify those priorities.The programme also showed how celebrity-led fundraising can mobilise attention quickly. Winfrey and Johnson’s involvement helped draw national attention to Maui’s recovery, while the involvement of local leaders and the Entertainment Industry Foundation helped turn that attention into a structured distribution system.A model for disaster recoveryThe People’s Fund of Maui was not intended to rebuild every destroyed home or replace every loss. It was designed as a bridge, providing direct financial support to families and individuals whose homes were lost or uninhabitable while they faced the immediate aftermath of the disaster.Its results offer a practical case study in rapid, community-informed relief. A clear eligibility rule, recurring payments, local application support, and public donations helped the fund move money to thousands of residents within weeks of the fires.For Maui survivors, the payments provided more than financial help. They also offered a measure of recognition that their losses were seen and that recovery would require sustained support from both local communities and people far beyond the island.You use AI every day. articles.title: A hidden air-raid shelter behind a garden hedge held decades-old wine worth £3.56 million, and 11 bottles of Romanee-Conti alone sold for £269,500 at Christie's London wine auction
articles.summary: England has become one of the most remarkable rare wine discoveries in recent auction history.
articles.body: England has become one of the most remarkable rare wine discoveries in recent auction history. Untouched for decades, the collection sold at Christie's London wine auction for £3.56 million, with every lot finding a buyer and several world records broken. Eleven bottles of Romanée-Conti 1971 alone fetched £269,500. If you are curious about valuable vintage wine, Burgundy, Bordeaux, champagne and port, read on to learn exactly how this hidden cellar was found, what treasures it held, and why it still matters for wine collectors.A surprise call from a couple who no longer drank led a Christie's specialist to a hidden shelterIn 2021, an out-of-the-blue telephone call from a couple who no longer really drank reached Noah May, head of Christie's Wine and Spirits department in London. It led to what he counts among his greatest discoveries. The bottles sat in a former air-raid shelter in southern England, reachable only through a thick hedge at the end of a garden. May told Christie's, in a story, about the auction house in May 2026 that the owner, who was in her eighties, worried about perishing labels and dusty conditions, and warned him not to get too excited. Her caution was understandable, since nobody could say what decades underground had done to the collection. Yet May went anyway, and what waited at the bottom of the stairs would change the expectations of everyone involved.Cases of Krug 1955 champagne, Quinta do Noval 1931 port and Mouton Rothschild 1945 lit by a phone torchAs May descended the staircase, the torchlight on his phone picked out one treasure after another. There were cases of Krug champagne from 1955, and Quinta do Noval port from 1931, along with various vintages of Domaine de la Romanée-Conti, La Tâche and Grands-Echézeaux. Then came eight bottles of Mouton Rothschild 1945, a wine May described to Christie's as arguably the greatest Bordeaux ever made. Stained labels, the very thing the owner had worried about, hinted at age rather than ruin. His reaction was immediate; May said he felt like "a poker player holding a royal flush." The moment shows why the discovery mattered so much. Champagne, port, Burgundy and claret of this calibre sat together in one forgotten room, untouched for decades.Bringing the collection to the surface and convincing its owner that stained labels were not a problemFinding the wine was only the beginning. May told Christie's that it took a long time to bring everything up to the surface, and even longer to convince the owner that the stained labels were not really an issue. In fact, he explained, the cellar had provided perfect conditions for storing wine. That was welcome news for an owner who had expected disappointment. What looked like neglect turned out to be an unexpectedly good home for wine, and the shelter had protected the bottles for decades. The collection was then offered in London in December 2021 under the title Treasures from a Rediscovered Chalk Cellar, a name that promised a story as much as a sale. Patience, in other words, was as important as expertise.Every lot sold for £3,556,396, more than double the combined low estimate, and world records fellThe result was emphatic. Christie's reports that every single lot sold, realising a total of £3,556,396, which is roughly £3.56 million and more than double the combined low estimate, while breaking several world records in the process. Leading the collection were 11 bottles of Romanée-Conti 1971, which realised £269,500 on their own. That outcome would have seemed unlikely to an owner who had warned the specialist not to get too excited. For a collection that spent decades behind a hedge, it was a remarkable return to public view. The owner's fears about perishing labels and dusty conditions proved unfounded. It also shows how much value can wait in places nobody thinks to look, and how a single telephone call can turn dusty bottles into a landmark sale.Could a forgotten luxury treasure be hidden in your home? Christie's advice to first-time sellersMay's discovery sits within a wider story. According to Christie's, its luxury category, which spans jewellery, handbags and accessories, watches, and wine and spirits, was the main entry point for new buyers in 2025 and achieved a combined total of $795 million. Rahul Kadakia, head of Global Luxury, told Christie's that its varied, relevant selection keeps drawing newer, younger buyers, particularly in luxury sales and among clients in the Asia-Pacific region. Christie's says prospective clients can request a complimentary estimate, provided the property meets the minimum consignment value, by telephone, Instagram, in person or through its online estimate service. If a forgotten cellar behind a hedge can hold more than three and a half million pounds of wine, it may be worth looking at what sits in your own attic.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: In 2025, France put eight wheeled solar panels directly on unused railway rails near Paris, testing whether the reversible setup could power maintenance sites without permanent construction
articles.summary: In a groundbreaking initiative, France has installed eight-wheeled solar panels on abandoned railway tracks to assess their potential as mobile power sources for railway operations, aiming for sustainability without permanent infrastructure.
articles.body: Railway companies own vast tracts of land, and some of it is track that trains no longer use. For a big electricity user, that raises an obvious question about whether those idle rails could earn their keep. SNCF, the national operator of France, has begun to ask whether they could serve as small power plants, and its engineers started answering in a very literal way in January 2025. At the Achères technical centre in the Yvelines department, west of Paris, eight solar panels mounted on wheels were installed straight onto an underused track and left to produce electricity for a six-month trial. The SNCF Group describes the system, called SOLVEIG, as fully reversible, with no groundwork or permanent anchoring, since the track itself serves as the foundation.How SOLVEIG workSOLVEIG was developed by AREP, SNCF’s multidisciplinary design agency, in partnership with the group’s technology and innovation departments and its renewables business, SNCF Renouvelables. According to PV magazine, the panels travel in a standard shipping container together with inverters and storage batteries, and a telescopic arm places them on the track. None of it is dug in, permanently anchored, or set in concrete, so the equipment can be removed from the track and moved elsewhere.Why reversibility mattersReversibility is the key feature. A traditional ground-mounted solar farm requires foundations and a lengthy approval process. AREP says its technology decreases the footprint on the land and the formalities needed to put it in place, which is important on a railway network that may want a dormant line back in service one day. AREP is also working on solar mapping of SNCF land, along with solar canopies and platform shelters. SOLVEIG is part of a broader effort rather than an isolated project.If the trial succeeds, the technology could be extended to underused lines across France to power nearby maintenance sites or support railway operations. The project manager, Astrid Parakenings, calls the broader concept ferrovoltaics. The long-term aim is to identify railway sites with high solar potential and turn idle tracks into sources of renewable energy.Why SNCF is trialling itSNCF, France’s biggest electricity consumer and second biggest property owner, is facing a high power bill and a lot of land. The SNCF Group is targeting 1,000 megawatts of peak solar capacity on its available land by 2030, enough to meet 15% to 20% of its current electricity needs. In July 2023, it launched SNCF Renouvelables to find appropriate sites for solar and ferrovoltaic projects, including derelict railway land. The eight panels at Achères are a tiny fraction of that goal, but they test an idea that could be replicated over many kilometres of inactive rail.The trial at Achères was due to run through June 2025, but detailed results were not available at the time of writing. That leaves open how much power the panels actually produced and how they coped with dust, weather and the tough conditions of a working rail site. Those figures will decide whether SOLVEIG moves beyond the prototype phase.A Swiss pilot on active tracksSOLVEIG is not the only version of this idea SNCF is following. Swiss company Sun-Ways is testing removable panels between the rails of a line that passenger trains still use, and the SNCF Group has joined as a partner to learn from the results. According to SNCF, the pilot will run until April 2028 while teams assess installation, glare, track inspection, maintenance impact, power output and dirt buildup. The setup uses 48 panels of 380 watts each, about 18 kilowatts peak in total, laid over a 100 metre stretch at Buttes in the canton of Neuchâtel since 24 April 2025. The two projects are testing different questions. SOLVEIG is installed on abandoned rail lines, while the Swiss design operates alongside active traffic.In short, France has placed a detachable solar plant on an unused railway track near Paris to test whether idle rails can power railway operations without permanent construction. The six-month test was scheduled to wrap up by June 2025, but detailed performance figures had not been made public at the time of writing, so ferrovoltaics remains a promising prototype rather than a standard way for railways to generate their own electricity.You use AI every day. articles.title: Man who fell off rollercoaster identified as Atlanta school teacher
articles.summary: Atlanta-area teacher and father of two fell to his death while riding hypercoaster Goliath at Georgia theme park.
articles.body:
See more Toronto Sun on Google — save as a Preferred Source

The man who fell to his death while riding a rollercoaster at a Georgia theme park has been identified as a school teacher from the Atlanta area.

Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, 42, died after falling 60 metres off the enormous Goliath rollercoaster at Six Flags Over Georgia amusement park on Monday, 11Alive local news reports . His family called him a "passionate educator" who loved his city of Atlanta, the outlet said.

According to WSB-TV News in Atlanta, Kariem recovered from cancer, and he and his daughter survived a car fire weeks before his death.

Kariem was on the ride with his son while his wife and daughter watched from the ground when he was thrown out of his seat and struck the coaster train three times before finally plummeting to his death, witnesses said.

The fall was disturbingly captured on an on-ride souvenir photo as Kariem tumbled over horrified, blood-covered guests on the ride.

"He was in our pictures," a witness told 11Alive. "He fell and hit the car three different times."

Another man and woman on the ride saw Kariem's fall firsthand and up close.

"We were having a great time and to just screaming, 'Oh my God, what is happening?'" the woman said.

The accident left another train of riders behind the affected coaster stuck on Goliath's steep 60-metre lift hill incline. The park was evacuated and workers carefully rescued riders off of the coaster and down the steep, open-air stairwell leading down to the ground.

Six Flags, which also owns and operates Canada's Wonderland, issued a statement shortly after the accident.

"We are deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today. Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the guest's family, friends, and loved ones. We are also providing support to the guests and team members affected.

"The park team and local authorities responded immediately, and we are cooperating fully with local authorities as they complete their investigation. Out of respect for the family's privacy, we will not be sharing additional details at this time."

Following the deadly accident in Georgia, Canada's Wonderland closed its two biggest rollercoasters, Behemoth and Leviathan, "out of an abundance of caution." Similar rides across Six Flags parks have also closed.

"The safety of our guests and team members remains one of our highest priorities," Six Flags added in a statement to the Sun .

Goliath was manufactured by Bollinger and Mabillard and is classified as a "hypercoaster" — a roller coaster that stands between 60 and 91 metres tall and reaches speeds of up to 112 km/h. Wonderland's Behemoth is slightly larger and faster, at 70 metres tall with a top speed of 123 km/h.

Wonderland's Leviathan tops them both. Classified as a Bollinger and Mabillard gigacoaster (a rollercoaster that reaches 91 metres or taller), it stands at 93 metres, making it Canada's tallest rollercoaster and one of the top 10 tallest rollercoasters in the world, with a top speed of 148 km/h.

Statistically, rollercoasters are very safe, but that doesn't mean accidents don't happen, and they can be deadly.

X2 (2026) – The world's first "fourth-dimensional" roller coaster ride at Six Flags Magic Mountain in California was linked to two deaths and a number of other serious injuries, particularly brain hemorrhages, according to CNN . Further investigation revealed at least 70 more injury complaints linked to the ride, many of them brain injuries.

The Smiler (2015) – One of the worst rollercoaster accidents in British history, a coaster train carrying 16 people on this ride at Alton Towers theme park in England slammed into a vacant, stalled test train at high speed. Passengers were trapped 7.6 metres in the air for more than four hours before emergency crews rescued them. All 16 passengers were injured, five seriously . Two young women suffered severe leg injuries and required leg amputations above the knee. Another rider suffered shattered kneecaps, severe lacerations and broken bones.

Big Thunder Mountain Railroad (2003) – Marcelo Torres, 22. died on this ride at Disneyland in California. He was riding in the front car when the locomotive separated from the rest of the cars and derailed. Torres bled to death after suffering blunt force trauma to the chest. He died at the scene and 10 other people were injured.

Mindbender (1986) – This rollercoaster at West Edmonton Mall in Edmonton derailed after cap screws holding the wheel assembly on a car failed. The rear car flew off the tracks at 100 km/h and struck a pillar, throwing four riders to the concrete floor below. David Sager, 24, Tony Andrusiak, 24, and his fiancée Cindy Sims, 21, were all killed. Rod Chayko survived, but has sustained injuries he'll deal with for the rest of his life.

articles.title: In 1990, Wisconsin built a test embankment for a gravel road over shredded waste tyres; after a year, inspectors rated its drainage excellent and called it among the better gravel roads
articles.summary: Discover how Wisconsin's use of shredded waste tires in road construction has proven to be effective, showcasing excellent drainage and durability, while providing an eco-friendly solution to tire waste.
articles.body: Millions of cars approach the end of their useful life each year, leaving behind an issue that is difficult to ignore. A tyre resists crushing, burns poorly, and does not lie neatly in a landfill because it is a tangle of rubber, synthetic fibre, and steel wire. As whole tyres became difficult to dispose of in sanitary landfills, stockpiles grew. A research paper by the University of Wisconsin–Madison team estimated that Wisconsin had about 20 million waste tyres stockpiled, with another 4 million generated each year. Engineers at the University of Wisconsin–Madison investigated whether shredded tyres could serve as fill beneath roads instead.So they built a test in 1990 to find out. The results, published in Transportation Research Record by Peter J. Bosscher, Tuncer B. Edil and Neil N. Eldin, documented the construction and performance of a gravel road embankment built using shredded waste tyres. After the first year, inspectors gave the embankment a strong assessment for drainage and described its overall performance as comparable to that of many gravel roads. The actual report is more cautious than that title, showing both what tyre chips can do and where they need support.A test embankment built beside a landfillThe test site was a small embankment beside the access road to the Dane County landfill near Madison, Wisconsin. It consisted of eight pieces, each 20 feet (approximately 6 metres) long and towering about 6 feet (1.8 metres) high with a 16-foot (4.9 metre) crest. Six portions behaved differently with tyre chips. Some used pure chips, one used half chips and half sand by volume, and one used alternate layers of chips and sand. Two portions were built of reinforced soil for comparison. The road also had approaches of pure earth.The researchers deliberately chose a severe environment. The embankment was exposed to heavy refuse-truck traffic from the landfill, allowing the researchers to observe how the different sections performed under repeated loading. The researchers obtained tyre chips from Wisconsin shredding plants. The paper reported processing costs of $30 to $65 per ton and noted that a ton of tyres represented approximately 100 tyres, although the exact weight and volume of shredded material varied with tyre size and chip characteristics.The Wisconsin findings are consistent with the broader engineering interest in using shredded tyres as lightweight fill. The Federal Highway Administration has documented their use in embankments and other highway applications, where their low unit weight and drainage properties can be useful. However, their suitability depends on the design, the amount of soil cover and how effectively the chips are confined.What the inspectors discoveredThe first couple of months were hard. Heavy truck traffic damaged the surface within days of opening, prompting crews to add crushed rock and regrade the road. Through the summer, the rutting, potholes, closure and regrading cycle repeated. The west approach, which was soil with no tyre chips at all, was badly damaged. Crews later applied calcium chloride to control dust. The road closed for the winter in December 1990 after a heavy snowfall.A formal inspection took place on 5 April 1991.The PASER system is a visual road-rating method described in a University of Wisconsin manual for gravel roads. The Wisconsin Department of Transportation district maintenance supervisor and university staff employed the PASER system. The writers believed that, following the initial time of adjustment and maintenance, the road was one of the better gravel roads. Because the sections were regraded before the subsequent rating, the perfect scores should be read in the context of that maintenance rather than as evidence that the road surface had remained undamaged throughout the trial.Tire chips provide a natural drainage advantage. Shreds and chips drain nearly as freely as clean gravel, says the Federal Highway Administration, which counts Wisconsin among at least 15 US states that have utilised them as lightweight fill in embankments.What the results tell us and don't tell usThe inspection results need to be interpreted in context because the road included both tyre-chip sections and approaches made from ordinary soil. The overall rating therefore cannot be attributed to the tyre chips alone. The researchers also found that settlement varied with the section's composition and the thickness of its soil cover. The best performers in the settlement measurements were the soil-only and fibre-reinforced sections. The parts with a 3-foot-thick soil cap and the chip and soil mix followed. The pure chip parts with only around 1 foot of cover did worse, perhaps due to the surface chips not being properly contained. The layered section did the worst of all. The authors concluded modestly. Once it has settled in, a gravel road made on tire chips operates like most gravel roads.The environmental outcomes were encouraging. The State Laboratory of Hygiene has tested shredded automobile tires and found no possibility of them becoming hazardous waste. In the lysimeters under the tire parts, the water stayed close to a neutral pH of around 7.5, and the sole elevated measurement was manganese, which the researchers attributed to local geology. They found that the tires probably would not contaminate groundwater.Wisconsin’s finding is in line with experience elsewhere. The Vermont Agency of Transportation reports that a town road in Vermont, built on a layer of tyre chips, is free of the spring muck that had plagued it, with the chip layer shutting off the rise of groundwater. Both situations demonstrate that tyre chips are suitable for roadways if drainage and cost are considerations and loads are regulated.The Wisconsin experiment showed that shredded waste tyres can serve as lightweight, free-draining fill beneath a gravel road, provided engineers contain the material properly and use adequate soil cover. The trial also revealed practical limitations: tyre chips were difficult to compact, exposed steel wires could puncture vehicle tyres, and the road required maintenance under heavy traffic. The findings support the use of shredded tyres in suitable embankment applications, but they do not establish that tyre chips alone produce a superior road surface.You use AI every day. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Congress on Tuesday hit back at Union home minister Amit Shah over his prediction of a resounding victory for the BJP-led NDA in the 2029 Lok
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress on Tuesday hit back at Union home minister Amit Shah over his prediction of a resounding victory for the BJP-led NDA in the 2029 Lok Sabha elections. Taking a dig at Shah, Congress general secretary KC Venugopal described his remarks as the “heights of irony”, questioning why the home minister was celebrating electoral victories while the opposition was protesting against alleged irregularities in the electoral system.“Heights of irony that Vote Chor Amit Shah is celebrating an election victory - when the whole problem is how they are destroying our electoral system,” Venugopal wrote on X.He also questioned Shah's focus on the 2029 elections, claiming that the home minister's remarks reflected concerns about Prime Minister Narendra Modi's political position. Venugopal further alleged that Shah appeared nervous during his interaction with the media, claiming that he spoke only to what he called “Godi media” and did not take questions.“Mr. Shah, you should certainly be worried about surviving in office till 2029,” Venugopal added.Congress leader Jairam Ramesh also targeted Shah, reviving the opposition's allegations of vote theft and accusing the home minister of relying on rhetoric rather than addressing concerns over the electoral process.“The Union home minister is back with his 3 Bs—Bombast, Bluff and Bluster,” Ramesh wrote on X.Calling Shah the “co-architect of Vote Chori”, Ramesh alleged that the BJP had already begun preparing to manipulate the 2029 elections.“The people know that the Constitutional right vote is their biggest power to hold authoritarian governments built on lies - like this one - accountable and send them packing,” he wrote, adding that the youth were among those taking to the streets.The Congress leaders' remarks came after Shah, in his first comments on the ongoing protests demanding chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation and the scrapping of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, predicted another crushing defeat for the Congress in 2029.Shah accused Rahul Gandhi and the opposition of pursuing negative politics, arguing that the Congress needed to introspect over its repeated electoral defeats. He maintained that voters continued to support PM Modi, the BJP and the NDA, citing recent bypolls and local body election results as evidence.Opposition leaders, including Rahul and Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge, joined INDIA bloc allies in a march for democracy in Delhi on Monday and vowed to continue their resistance against alleged electoral irregularities.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2024, a Pennsylvania dairy farmer cut his monthly power bill from $2,500 to $74 by putting solar panels on his barn, whilecontinuing to carefor 300 cows
articles.summary: Discover how Richard Perkoski, a Pennsylvania dairy farmer, dramatically reduced his monthly electricity bill from $2,500 to $74 by installing solar panels on his barn. Supported by a USDA grant, this sustainable energy approach enables him to maintain his farm operations efficiently while considering expansion options.
articles.body: A Pennsylvania dairy farmer says he decreased his monthly electricity bill from $2,500 to $74,following the installation of solar panels on his barn roof. According to the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette, Richard Perkoski, owner of Main Street Milk, said the installation was funded through a grant from the US Department of Agriculture’s Rural Energy for America Program (REAP). The savings have helped him free up money for farm needs while the operation continues to milk cows and grow crops with five people employed in the workforce. The cost for installing the 321 solar panels came to $284,000, of which the USDA grant covered $110,208,while Perkoski paid the remaining $174,000.How the solar panels supply the dairy By generating power on site, the panels have substantially reduced the farm’s electricity costs. Electricity is the backbone of the farm's daily operations; it drives the milking equipment and vacuum pumps. Simultaneously, it keeps the lights on, handles the heating, and powers the massive cooling systems required to keep the milk at the perfect temperature. When the panels generate more electricity than the farm requires, surplus power is returned to the grid in exchange for utility credits. These credits help to reduce electricity drawn from the grid in case the solar production falls.At full capacity, the panels are capable of producing energy for around eight months of the year; conversely, their lower output can last up to four months. Perkoski runs the 590-acre farm with 300 cows, milking 220 of them, while growing corn and hay. With his ongoing savings, he has purchased additional barn lighting and hopes to expand the herd and transition to electric tractors.As per Farm and Dairy, Perkoski’s dairy installation comes from his wider experience with solar energy, which began around 15 years earlier when he installed 200 panels at his home. Later in 2021, he began a separate solar farm on 48 acres with 8,000 ground-mounted panels in Jefferson Hills, Pennsylvania, which supplied electricity to Duquesne Light Company.How USDA funding supports farm energy projects In October 2024, the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) announced an additional $104 million in Rural Energy for America Program (REAP) grants to support more than 300 clean-energy projects across 34 states. The programme's objective was to help agricultural producers and rural small businesses invest in renewable-energy systems and energy-efficiency improvements.REAP was established through the 2008 Farm Bill, which initially received $255 million in funding. Farm and Dairy reported that the Inflation Reduction Act, passed in 2022, subsequently provided more than $2.3 billion in additional investment for the programme. The funding also extends to energy systems that use agricultural waste. The USDA estimates the project could generate 2.7 million kilowatt-hours of electricity annually, equivalent to the power used by 252 homes of electricity annually, equivalent to the power used by 252 homes. Anaerobic digesters process organic material, including farm waste, to produce biogas that can be used for energy. Replacing the engine was intended to support the farm’s ability to generate electricity from this system. These projects show the various ways REAP funding can help farms address energy costs while maintaining equipment that converts agricultural waste into power.You use AI every day. articles.title: Canadian former NHLer Ron Duguay's family gives update amid his stage 4 cancer fight: 'We need all the prayers we can get'
articles.summary: "I know so many love him so much."
articles.body:
Former NHL star Ron Duguay's daughter gave a rare update on her father's battle with stage 4 colon cancer. On Sunday, Duguay's daughter, Shay Thomas, shared a black and white photo of herself sitting beside her father's hospital bed.

"I wasn't planning on posting anything. but I believe in the power of prayer, and right now, we need all the prayers we can get," the caption read. "And I know so many love him so much. Please keep our dad in your prayers."

In February 2026, Duguay's revealed that he had been living with stage 4 colon cancer for about a year. The athlete's family launched a GoFundMe to help offset medical costs which required Duguay to travel from his home in Florida to Orange County, Calif. for treatment every two weeks.

"I had a little something in my colon, that ended up in my liver. I had no idea," Duguay said during an interview with Sid Rosenberg in the Sid & Friends in the Morning radio show in February.

Duguay lives in Florida near his son, Noah, has been leaning heavily on his family for support. He said his daughters, Thomas and Amber Stavros, who live in California, "took charge" of his treatment.

"They would just lift me up…," he said. "That's what's important. You can't go negative. It's all positive. It's all good. They just put life into me and they just adore their dad and I love them back — it's been wonderful."

Duguay, who also has a son named Noah, has been leaning heavily on his family for support, along with Sarah Palin, former governor of Alaska, his partner since 2022.

In July, Duguay, who played in the NHL from 1977 to 1989, was hospitalized after fainting in his home. He was found unconscious and lost some teeth as a result of his fall.

"After extensive testing, doctors found that he was extremely dehydrated and had been struggling to eat because of how sick he had been feeling," Thomas wrote in a social media update. "They also discovered varices, portal hypertensive gastropathy, internal bleeding, and an ulcer."

On Aug. 25, Thomas shared an update on her dad's health in a lengthy Instagram post after Duguay underwent a round of treatment.

"He still has a lot of healing ahead," she wrote adding that her dad "continues to smile" and "crack his jokes."

"We are beyond grateful for every prayer, donation, message and support! I love all the old pics people send me of my dad! So continue to do so! This journey has been such a roller coaster, but through every high and low, we continue to put our trust in God and stay grateful for every bit of progress. Thank you so much for continuing to support and pray for him."

articles.title: Years after Andre the Giant’s death, his former 46-acre North Carolina estate went to auction, with parts of the home custom-built for his 7-foot-4 frame
articles.summary: Explore the auction of André the Giant's 46-acre estate in North Carolina, featuring a custom-built home and unique accommodations for the wrestling legend. Discover how the property changed hands after failing to meet the reserve price in November 2013.
articles.body: André the Giant had spent the final decade of his life in his North Carolina property before it went up for auction. The estate in Ellerbe covered about 46 acres and included a three-story, roughly 3,500-square-foot house, two natural streams, a barbecue building, gazebo and workshop. André Roussimoff, the French-born wrestler known worldwide as André the Giant, had lived there during the later years of his career.The property went on the auction block in November 2013, two decades after Roussimoff's death in 1993. The auction drew two main bidders, but neither reached the owners' undisclosed reserve price, and the property eventually changed hands through post-auction negotiations.The house was not entirely built for a giantStories about André's North Carolina home often describe it as a house that was constructed entirely around his enormous size, but the reality was more specific. The Charlotte Observer reported that an oak tree once grew through the middle of the house and that André had a custom-built recliner. He also found it difficult to navigate parts of the house, with longtime ranchmate Jackie McAuley recalling that he sometimes had to turn his feet sideways to make it up a narrow staircase.Roussimoff stood about 7 feet 4 inches tall and weighed roughly 500 pounds during his wrestling career. A later account from CBS Sports reported that a plumber raised the shower head so that André could use it comfortably, while the household acquired two or three oversized chairs, and according to McAuley, those were among the few specific accommodations made for him. His size made ordinary houses, vehicles and furniture difficult to use, but the Ellerbe property gave him privacy, which he could not easily have while traveling the world for wrestling.The auction divided the estate into two separate parcelsThe 46 acres were divided into two parcels; one containing the house and about nine acres, and another consisting of roughly 37.7 acres of woodland, and that setup gave potential buyers the option of being able to pursue different parts of the estate instead of treating the property as a single residential purchase. The auction was handled by Swicegood Group and drew five registered bidders, although the contest ultimately narrowed to two main parties.Florida crime writer Randy Wayne White, who participated with his uncle, Levon Wilson, was interested in the property as a potential place to write, but he had also hoped it would include a lake or pond, and stopped bidding at $260,000. The other serious bidder was Rockingham resident George Ewing, who was prepared to go as high as $270,000. His bid still fell below the owners’ undisclosed reserve, so the property did not sell during the roughly 40-minute auction, with the property reportedly being assessed at $358,000 at the time.The auction company announced in January 2014 that the property had transferred to the highest bidder from the November auction after post-sale negotiations. The final sale price was not disclosed, which made the transaction less notable for a headline auction price than for the way the estate finally changed hands after the public bidding failed to reach the reserve.He spent his final years on the ranchNorth Carolina's Department of Natural and Cultural Resources says that Roussimoff had purchased nine acres in the Ellerbe area in 1978 and expanded his holdings over the following decade to a 194-acre ranch along Big Mountain Creek. The 46-acre property that was later offered at auction was therefore only part of the larger landholding that he was associated with. The ranch became a place where Roussimoff could spend time away from wrestling crowds, and the Charlotte Observer reported that he rode a Honda three-wheeler around the property, raised Texas longhorns and entertained wrestling friends there. After his death in France in 1993, his ashes were returned to the North Carolina ranch.The property continued through several owners before the 2013 auction, with the auction listing describing the house as a three-story residence with four bedrooms, three bathrooms, two dens and a two-car garage, along with the separate structures on the wooded acreage. North Carolina dedicated a highway historical marker to Roussimoff in Ellerbe in April 2026, and recognised his connection to the community and the ranch where he spent much of the last 15 years of his life.You use AI every day. articles.title: Pakistani student killed while ‘praying’ on road, driver avoids jail in Australia
articles.summary: A 20-year-old driver in Australia has avoided jail after hitting and killing an international student who was kneeling in the middle of a road with her
articles.body: A 20-year-old driver in Australia has avoided jail after hitting and killing an international student who was kneeling in the middle of a road with her hands in what appeared to be a praying motion, before leaving the scene of the accident.Ashton Friend, from Banksia Park, had pleaded guilty to causing death by careless use of a motor vehicle and leaving the scene of an accident following the death of 20-year-old Samia Malik on North East Road in Hillcrest, Adelaide, on May 6, 2025.The South Australian District Court heard that Malik had been kneeling in the middle of the road for around four minutes before Friend's car struck her at about 11pm. CCTV footage showed her hands in what appeared to be a "praying motion", Judge Anne Barnett said while sentencing Friend on Tuesday. No explanation has been provided for why Malik was on the road.Friend was driving home from his girlfriend's house when the collision occurred. According to his defence barrister, Jane Abbey KC, he had not seen Malik and did not realise he had hit a person."He was absolutely at a loss about what had just happened. He hadn't been aware that there was something on the road. He heard this noise," Abbey told the court. "What he hoped was that it had been an animal, or something like that."Abbey said the relatively limited damage to Friend's car had contributed to his failure to realise that he had struck someone. He later learnt about Malik's death through news reports and was left in a "state of paralysis", the court heard.Friend had previously expressed remorse for his actions in an apology to the court, saying: "I will have to carry my failures with me for as long as I live."Judge Barnett sentenced him to one year, three months and 29 days in prison, with a non-parole period of eight months. However, the sentence was suspended after Friend entered a bond requiring him to be of good behaviour for two years, allowing him to avoid immediate imprisonment.Malik was an international student studying in Australia, with her family in Pakistan.You use AI every day. articles.title: She fled Ukraine to safety in Alberta. Now, she’s worried about her place after the referendum
articles.summary: Ukrainians in Alberta fear what the outcome of the immigration questions in the referendum could mean for their standing in the province they now call home.
articles.body:
When Anna Tselukhina first read the five immigration-related questions Alberta put on the Oct. 19 referendum ballot, she felt her family's future plunge into "total uncertainty."

Since 2022, the mother of two has been living in Calgary, along with thousands of other Ukrainians who were welcomed here while Russia continues its war with her homeland. Now, she and her family are facing new unknowns.

"Will the war in Ukraine stop in the nearest future? We don't know. Will we get permanent residency here in Canada soon? We don't know. Will we have to pay for medical insurance? For education? We don't know," she said.

"A lot of that we don't know. And nobody knows so far."

The current president of the local Ukrainian Canadian Congress branch arrived in Calgary through a federal government program after fleeing Sievierodonetsk, a city in eastern Ukraine now under Russian military occupation.

Now, Tselukhina fears what the outcome of the immigration questions in the referendum could mean for her and her family's standing in the province they now call home.

The upcoming referendum poses 10 questions to Albertans, including one on whether the province should hold a binding referendum to separate from Canada, and five immigration-related questions that could impact tens of thousands of non-permanent residents.

Those questions propose limiting eligibility to public services, instituting a 12-month waiting period before non-permanent residents can access social programs, and introducing a mandatory fee for access to public health care and education, among others.

"That would be a huge question whether we'll be able to afford to pay for [our kids'] education if people will vote yes to those questions and of course, this just adds to the overall anxiety that we have," Tselukhina said.

In Calgary, Tselukhina works as a kitchen manager in a fast food restaurant, and her partner works as a caregiver. Their children have fully integrated into life in Canada, Tselukhina said.

While the couple's financial situation makes it possible to make ends meet for now, Tselukhina said the prospect of having to pay extra for public services could force them to move to a different province.

" I hate to say that we will have to consider moving from here because we don't wanna move. We love it here. We love Calgary, and our children, they love it here, and they love school. But I don't know if it will be possible for us to afford everything."

LISTEN | The stakes of Alberta's referendum questions on immigration:

Most Ukrainians who arrived in Canada after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine came under a federal program called the Canada–Ukraine Authorization for Emergency Travel (CUAET).

It was a temporary measure meant to fast-track their arrival to Canada so those escaping the war wouldn't have to go through the usual, often slow refugee process. Approximately 300,000 Ukrainians arrived in Canada after Russia launched its invasion on Feb. 24, 2022.

The CUAET visa does not offer a direct pathway to permanent residency.

A spokesperson for Lena Metlege Diab, the federal Minister of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship, said as of July 31, there are about 43,500 temporary residents in Alberta whose country of citizenship is Ukraine, according to preliminary data.

That number includes Ukrainians who arrived under CUAET and other pathways. Of those, about 6,500 have applied for permanent residency.

In February, Canada's immigration department said it expects Ukrainians who fled the war with Russia to return to their home country once the conflict ends. But with the war showing no signs of ending, many of those Ukrainians are hoping to make Canada a permanent home.

Now, people like Tselukhina are left in a limbo — and it's why the referendum's five questions on immigration are so worrying.

A 'huge hurdle' for Ukrainian immigrants

With the vote looming, Calgary-based immigration consultant Tetiana Karbovanets is hearing concerns from several of her Ukrainian clients.

Many of them, she said, are worried about how their access to free public health care and education may change depending on the outcome of the referendum.

Question four of the referendum proposes charging non-permanent residents a "reasonable fee or premium" for their and their family's use of the public health care and education systems.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith has said her government is considering charging temporary residents a $1,900 fee akin to a premium charged in the United Kingdom for access to public health care.

"A lot of Ukrainians are struggling [in Alberta]. They are having, like, low-paid positions … So this is a huge concern for them, hearing those questions about temporary residents losing access to education," Karbovanets said.

"For some people, it would be a huge hurdle in that situation as they are not making enough here and they have no other options. They already built some life here, they adjusted, their children — usually smaller children — go to schools here.

"So starting over after what they went through in Ukraine, it would be devastating for them."

If the public health and education fee is implemented and applied to Ukrainians, Karbovanets said, some Ukrainians may have to consider moving to another province as life would become too expensive for them.

Province doesn't say which residents could be impacted

The second of five immigration questions suggests only giving certain non-permanent residents with an "Alberta-approved immigration status" access to public health care and education altogether.

That designation doesn't currently exist. When asked by CBC News to define the term on several occasions, the province has consistently said it will be decided in the legislature after the vote.

But knowing the answer now is critical for immigrants like Tselukhina, as she contemplates her and her family's future in Alberta.

Alberta's Minister of Jobs, Economy, Trade and Immigration Joseph Schow didn't commit to an answer on whether Ukrainians would count as an "Alberta-approved" immigrant when asked by The Sunday Magazine host Piya Chattopadhyay.

"What I'm saying is that no one's going to be left out, but we are going to make sure that things are sustainable," Schow said.

"I want to go back to the main point of this, which is ensuring that we, as our burdens, have an immigration program that works for Alberta. You know, we continue to attract investment from all over the world. We have labour demands that need to be met, and some of those labour demands cannot be met by people yet."

Schow also did not say whether any of these policies would affect only new temporary residents, or if they would also apply to current temporary residents already in the province.

"A lot of people forget that Ukrainians who came through these programs, they are here on a temporary status." Karbovanets said.

"They are not refugees … They're evacuees, but they only have temporary status and they are in the same situation as anyone else. They have to pay their taxes, they have to pay for their housing. They don't have any additional supports."

Even if Ukrainians are exempted from new fees, Mariana Sirko, a cultural coordinator with the European Cultural Society of Calgary — who arrived in Alberta from Kyiv in 2024 — worries a system that singles out one group could breed division amongst diasporic communities.

"If Ukrainians will be picked up in this process, we could be relieved because of our personal reasons, but we still will be uncomfortable regarding the relationships with other groups," Sirko said.

"Because, of course, the situation of picking someone will create questions between different groups and throughout the time, those prejudices could grow. We want to live with mutual support and respect with other groups."

Tselukhina said when it is so unclear whether Ukrainian immigrants will continue to access public and social services the way they do now, it's hard to keep calm amidst the uncertainty.

"You just depend on the results of the voting and then you still depend on the officials because obviously it will be them who will decide who will be included in that group, who will be exempt from any kind of influence of the results of this referendum."

articles.title: In 2022, California's 4.2-acre Rancho Cariñoso asked $109 million; after years of price cuts, the beachfront horse ranch sold at auction for $22.55 million, with nearly an acre of private beach
articles.summary: Once marketed for $109 million, Rancho Cariñoso has sold at auction for $22.55 million, a dramatic drop for a property with nearly an acre of private
articles.body: Once marketed for $109 million, Rancho Cariñoso has sold at auction for $22.55 million, a dramatic drop for a property with nearly an acre of private beach. The 4.2-acre estate sits on Padaro Lane, between Carpinteria and Santa Barbara, and combines a working horse-ranch character with rare oceanfront access. Its features include a three-bedroom home, citrus and avocado groves, equestrian trails leading to the sand and access to the Loon Point surf break. Realtor.com reported that the property had spent years on and off the market, with its asking price repeatedly reduced before it went to auction. The sale closes a long search for a buyer willing to take on one of Southern California’s most distinctive coastal estates.A ranch beside the PacificRancho Cariñoso occupies a coveted stretch of coastline near Loon Point Beach. The property’s 4.2 acres include almost an acre of private beachfront, a rare feature in a region where oceanfront homes are often tightly packed together. Its mix of open land, shoreline and equestrian facilities gives it a character quite different from a typical coastal mansion.The estate is designed around its owner’s access to the outdoors. Horse trails and ATV paths run across the property, with routes leading directly to the sand. The estate also includes access to the Loon Point surf break, while yacht owners can use offshore dockage with tender access.The property is zoned for as many as nine horses, making it especially appealing to equestrian buyers. It is also a short distance from the Santa Barbara Polo Club, an added draw for polo enthusiasts. The result is a property where riding, surfing, boating and beach walks can all be part of daily life.A modest house on extraordinary landDespite the estate’s enormous price history, the main residence is relatively restrained. The 2,500-square-foot home has three bedrooms and was built in 2014. A detached garage measures about 1,000 square feet, while additional build-ready sites offer room for future structures or amenities. The grounds include avocado and citrus groves, giving the estate a more rural feeling than many luxury homes in the area. The combination of productive land and a private beach sets Rancho Cariñoso apart from properties whose value rests mainly on the size of the house, as per the report.That balance was central to the way the property was marketed. The estate was not simply presented as a large residence with ocean views, but as an opportunity to own a private coastal ranch. Its land could support horses, outdoor recreation and additional development, while preserving the beach access and open space that make it distinctive.From $109 million to auctionRancho Cariñoso first reached the market in 2022 with an asking price of $109 million. That figure reflected the property’s rarity, but it proved difficult to match with a buyer. After being on and off the market for several years, it was relisted in 2024 for close to $70 million.The price continued to fall. By August 2026, the asking price had been reduced to $48.975 million. The estate was then taken to auction in September, with bids starting at $20 million. Concierge Auctions handled the sale, which closed at $22.55 million.The final price was about one-fifth of the original $109 million asking amount, it was shared in the report. It was also less than half the last reported list price. The gap illustrates the difference between a seller’s initial valuation and the amount buyers are ultimately willing to pay, particularly for a highly specialised property with an exceptionally high asking price.The sale does not necessarily mean the estate was worth only a fraction of its original asking price. Market conditions, timing, buyer interest and the auction process all influence the final result. But the substantial difference makes the transaction one of the most striking recent examples of a high-end California property changing hands well below its original target.A long family connectionThe property was sold by Arthur A. Cameron III, an oil heir and polo enthusiast. He inherited the ranch from his father, Arthur Cameron II, who bought the land in 1978 as part of a larger 28-acre acquisition for $1 million, according to information cited by Realtor.com.The property’s history helps explain its equestrian identity. Cameron’s interest in polo aligned with the land’s location near the Santa Barbara Polo Club, while the beach access and open acreage offered a lifestyle that is difficult to recreate elsewhere in Southern California.The property is also surrounded by high-profile neighbours. Realtor.com noted that Padaro Lane is home to celebrities including actor Kevin Costner, filmmaker George Lucas and reality television personality Kourtney Kardashian. Even in that setting, Rancho Cariñoso stands out because of its private beachfront and horse-riding access.A rare opportunity, at a new priceListing agent Barron Hilton described the estate as a place where an owner could ride horses onto the beach, surf a private break and enjoy oceanfront privacy across more than four acres. The estate’s additional build-ready sites also offered the possibility of adding to the property while preserving its existing character.The auction result gives the next owner a chance to decide what comes next. The existing home is relatively modest compared with the acreage, and the property has room for additional buildings or amenities, subject to applicable approvals. Its defining features, however, are already in place: private beach, trails, groves, ocean access and space for horses.At $22.55 million, Rancho Cariñoso has moved from an extraordinary $109 million listing to a sale price that remains within the realm of only a small pool of buyers. The figure is far below the original asking price, but the estate is still an unusual offering: a private coastal ranch where the beach is not just a view from the house, but part of the property itself.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: TOI explains: Why can’t Bengaluru protest outside Freedom Park?
articles.summary: A Karnataka high court order and a police licensing regime have made Freedom Park Bengaluru’s default protest venue.
articles.body: A Karnataka high court order and a police licensing regime have made Freedom Park Bengaluru’s default protest venue. But the governing police order also gives the police commissioner discretion to designate another suitable venue, meaning the legal position is more nuanced than an absolute ban on demonstrations elsewhere. Here’s everything you need to know about why Bengaluru cannot protest outside Freedom Park:Bengaluru has confined protests to Freedom Park. The practice emerged from a suo motu Karnataka High Court case initiated in 2021 over the effect of demonstrations on traffic and the rights of people not participating in them.How did the restriction begin?On March 3, 2022, a division bench of the Karnataka High Court passed an interim order directing the state government to ensure that no protests, processions and similar activities were held anywhere in Bengaluru except at Freedom Park, Gandhinagar. The court also directed that such activities be organised without adversely affecting traffic, especially during rush hours, and that action be taken where traffic was disrupted.On August 1, 2022, the High Court disposed of the case. In paragraph 4, it recorded a submission that protests, marches and dharnas would be permitted only at Freedom Park, and that the state was obliged to ensure compliance with the 2021 licensing order. In paragraph 5, the operative direction required authorities to ensure compliance with that order “in letter and spirit” and to continue action against those violating it.What does the police order say?The Licensing and Regulation of Protests, Demonstrations and Protest Marches (Bengaluru City) Order, 2021, published in the state gazette in January 2022, is the rule currently governing protests in Bengaluru. It says no protests, demonstrations, dharnas or protest marches may be held in the city without a licence under the order.Clause 4.1 identifies Freedom Park as the venue for protests in Bengaluru. However, it also says that, depending on the situation, the commissioner of police may designate any other suitable place in the city for that purpose. The licensing authority may approve the number of participants at Freedom Park based on the type of programme, duration and available capacity.So, are protests outside Freedom Park illegal?Not necessarily in every circumstance. The 2021 order does not expressly prohibit protest marches, nor does it state that Freedom Park is the only possible venue: it identifies Freedom Park while preserving the police commissioner’s discretion to designate another suitable location.A legal backgrounder prepared by activists argues that the High Court’s final order did not itself direct that protests be held only at Freedom Park; it directed compliance with the licensing order. On that reading, the court’s judgment does not prevent rallies and does not mandate Freedom Park as the sole venue.The distinction matters because the March 2022 interim order did expressly restrict protests and processions to Freedom Park, while the August 2022 final order required enforcement of the 2021 licensing rules. The two must be read alongside the licensing order before drawing a definitive legal conclusion.Why does this matter?Activists argue that concentrating demonstrations at one venue reduces their visibility and makes it harder for groups to draw public attention to local grievances. The backgrounder says the restrictions have affected workers, farmers, Dalit activists, sanitation workers and residents seeking to protest on issues in their own localities.The debate is ultimately about balancing traffic management and public convenience with the constitutional right to assemble peacefully and express dissent. For now, Freedom Park remains Bengaluru’s designated and practically dominant protest venue. articles.title: A billionaire who bought Tasmania’s Woolnorth dairy for A$280 million in 2016 has won a tax reversal: a full court overturned the case that had left his companies facing A$23.4 million including penalties and interest
articles.summary: A Full Court in Tasmania has overturned a multi-million-dollar tax assessment against companies linked to billionaire businessman Xianfeng Lu.
articles.body: A Full Court in Tasmania has overturned a multi-million-dollar tax assessment against companies linked to billionaire businessman Xianfeng Lu. The decision cancels a disputed A$23.4 million stamp duty bill, including accumulated penalties and interest. The ruling is a major legal win for Moon Lake Investments and other companies linked to Mr Lu. The dispute arose from the 2016 purchase of the large Woolnorth dairy estate in north-west Tasmania. Moon Lake Investments Pty Ltd bought the property for A$280 million.Background on the 2016 Woolnorth acquisitionXianfeng Lu bought the historic Woolnorth property in March 2016, adding the large farming business to his wider portfolio. The deal involved buying the assets of the Van Diemen's Land Company, one of Australia's largest and oldest dairy farming operations. When the deal was first settled in 2016, Van Dairy Limited paid A$8.2 million in standard stamp duty. However, tax authorities later argued that additional transactions and share transfers made before the deal was finalised meant more tax had to be paid. By July 2021, the Tasmanian State Revenue Office had informed lawyers representing the companies that further payments were due. The authority claimed that Ningbo Moon Lake Investment Company and Van Dairy Holdings Limited each owed separate amounts of stamp duty, along with penalty tax and interest. These charges pushed the total demand above A$20 million.Previous legal rulings and court appealsThe tax dispute moved through the courts over several years as the companies challenged the penalty assessments and the way the underlying tax amounts had been calculated. In November 2024, Acting Justice Shane Marshall rejected appeals from both sides during the first stage of the court case. This left the companies facing the large financial liability. Unhappy with the outcome, lawyers for Mr Lu's companies took the case to a Full Court for further review. On Wednesday, the Full Court delivered its final decision. The panel included Chief Justice Chris Shanahan, Justice Michael Brett, and Justice Stephen Estcourt. The judges ruled fully in favour of Mr Lu's investment companies. They also formally rejected a cross-appeal filed by the State Revenue Office.Impact on agricultural holdings and local operationsThe successful appeal removes a major financial burden that had hung over the companies managing the property in north-west Tasmania for years. Since the 2016 purchase, the large Woolnorth estate has gone through major changes in how it operates. Parts of the farming land were later sold to other agricultural groups, including sections bought by the TRT Pastoral Group in 2021. Sales involving the remaining land, livestock, machinery, and historical records linked to the Van Diemen's Land Company name have also continued. These sales have been listed through agency networks such as Nutrien Harcourts. Looking back on his time managing the property through various business and ownership changes, Mr Lu said in earlier public comments reported by Tasmanian Country that it had been an "honour to be the owner and custodian of one of Australia's most important historic agricultural properties." The latest court ruling provides legal certainty for the complex company transactions behind the multi-million-dollar agricultural purchase made nearly a decade ago. It also brings one of the most closely watched tax disputes in modern Tasmanian business history to a close.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: India reaffirms Ladakh status as China says it doesn’t recognise the UT
articles.summary: Diplomatic tensions flared again between India and China after Beijing strongly opposed India’s decision to officially map and standardise 28 places in
articles.body: Diplomatic tensions flared again between India and China after Beijing strongly opposed India’s decision to officially map and standardise 28 places in Ladakh, including some in Aksai China, and reaffirmed that it does not recognise the Union Territory (UT) of Ladakh.In a swift rebuttal, New Delhi reiterated no amount of Chinese denial can change the established fact that the Ladakh UT is an integral and inalienable part of India.According to the ministry of home affairs (MHA), which announced the standardisation in a press release on October 2, identifying the places/ geographical features formally on the Survey of India map was aimed at facilitating their accurate recognition and better awareness among the public at large. MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal reiterated the same, saying the MHA statement was self-explanatory.“The announcement mentions that the twenty-eight (28) places/features located in the UT of Ladakh have been identified with standard place and feature names on the official map of Survey of India, and it has been done in consultation with the Union Territory of Ladakh and local stakeholders,” he said.The Chinese foreign ministry described the Indian move as illegal saying it doesn’t change the fact that the western sector of the China-India boundary belongs to China. “China has never recognized the so-called Union Territory of Ladakh unilaterally and illegally established by India, and firmly opposes the so-called standardized names publicised by India,” said spokesperson Mao Ning.However, China itself has renamed places in Arunachal Pradesh on at least half a dozen occasions in the past 10 years, including twice in 2026, to reinforce its claim over the Indian state.The fresh cartographic tussle comes in the middle of the ongoing normalisation of the bilateral relationship after a military standoff in eastern Ladakh. The Chinese response was a throwback to its statement in 2019 – a day after India revoked the special status of J&K in 2019 – accusing New Delhi of undermining China's territorial sovereignty by unilaterally changing its domestic law and establishing Ladakh UT.“Such practice is unacceptable and will not come into force,” it had then said, warning India to exercise prudence in words and deeds on the boundary question. It was perhaps no coincidence that the military conflict in eastern Ladakh started 8 months later.Beijing maintains that it has always opposed India's inclusion of “Chinese territory in the western sector of the China-India boundary into its administrative jurisdiction”. For China, Aksai Chin in the western sector remains of critical importance as it links the politically sensitive autonomous regions of Xinjiang and Tibet.However, the border situation has remained stable since PM Narendra Modi and President Xi Jinping met in Kazan in 2024. India and China have since held 3 rounds of Special Representatives talks on the boundary question, with the last round in August resulting in 8 outcomes, including a decision to advance talks for an “early and substantial” harvest of boundary delimitation and border management.Get the latest India News and Live updates.
