articles.title: In 1994, Hamdi Ulukaya arrived in the US unable to speak English and knowing nobody; after building Chobani, he hired hundreds of refugees and migrants and built Tent into a 400+ company network helping newcomers find work
articles.summary: When Hamdi Ulukaya arrived in the United States in 1994, he was a young student from Turkey who spoke no English and knew no one.
articles.body: When Hamdi Ulukaya arrived in the United States in 1994, he was a young student from Turkey who spoke no English and knew no one. Years later, after buying a shuttered yogurt factory and building Chobani into a major business, he began hiring refugees and migrants, helping hundreds find work in the company’s plants. That experience inspired Tent, a business network Ulukaya founded in 2016 to encourage employers to hire refugees. The UN Refugee Agency, UNHCR, says Tent now connects with more than 400 companies across the Americas and Europe. Its work includes training, hiring guides and job fairs designed to help newcomers overcome barriers to employment. Ulukaya’s own journey, reported by CBS News, helps explain why he sees a first job as a vital step towards belonging.Starting over in a new countryUlukaya arrived in the US at 22, with little money and no English, according to a CBS News profile. He had left Turkey after facing questioning over his writing in support of Kurdish rights. In upstate New York, he spent years studying, working on a dairy farm and learning how to build a life in a place where he had no family or friends.His path into business began with a modest feta cheese company. Then he noticed an advertisement for a shuttered yogurt factory in New Berlin, New York. The plant had once employed about 200 people, but Kraft Foods had closed it. Ulukaya saw more than an old industrial building. He saw a chance to revive a workplace and bring jobs back to a community.He secured financing with support from a regional bank and the Small Business Administration, then reopened the factory as Chobani. His first hires included former employees of the closed plant. As the business grew, the company needed more workers, more milk from local dairy farms and additional production capacity.Hiring beyond language barriersChobani’s expansion brought Ulukaya into contact with a refugee resettlement centre in Utica, about 40 miles from the New Berlin factory. Staff told him that refugees were struggling to find work, in part because of language and transportation barriers. His response was practical: Chobani would provide interpreters and transport so people could get to the plant and do the job.The company went on to hire hundreds of refugees and migrants. UNHCR says Chobani has also offered English-language classes and access to translators who speak multiple languages. Those measures helped workers settle into a new workplace while allowing the company to draw on a wider pool of employees.In the CBS News report, Ulukaya described refugees as hardworking and loyal employees. He argued that a job could help newcomers become part of society after losing homes, family connections and familiar routines. Employment, in his view, was not only about earning wages. It could be a first step towards rebuilding a life.The approach grew out of the company’s needs, but it also reflected Ulukaya’s own experience as a newcomer. He knew what it meant to arrive without language or connections. At Chobani, he had the ability to change some of the conditions that might otherwise keep people from entering the workforce.Turning one company’s experience into TentIn 2016, Ulukaya founded the Tent Partnership for Refugees, seeking to encourage other employers to follow the hiring model he had developed at Chobani. The idea was to move refugee employment beyond the actions of a single company by mobilising businesses with the scale to create many more opportunities.UNHCR describes Tent as a network of more than 400 major companies committed to helping refugees enter local labour markets across a dozen countries in the Americas and Europe. The organisation works with employers on job-readiness and recruitment, while helping companies understand barriers such as limited access to job listings, vocational training, language services and work permits.Tent’s work includes practical tools for businesses. UNHCR says the partnership has produced hiring guides for countries including Spain, Mexico and France, and organised job fairs that connect refugees with employers. The organisations have also advocated for policy changes that could make formal employment more accessible.In 2023, Tent and its partners made a pledge on economic inclusion and social protection at the Global Refugee Forum. The wider ambition is to make refugee hiring part of business practice, rather than an occasional charitable gesture.A partnership with UNHCRUNHCR and Tent formalised a partnership to connect refugees with employment opportunities, including through the network of more than 400 companies. The agreement builds on years of collaboration between the two organisations on hiring resources and job fairs.The partnership recognises that refugees face barriers beyond the process of applying for a job. People may need help understanding the local labour market, gaining relevant skills, finding employers willing to consider their experience and navigating work-permit rules. Businesses may also need guidance on recruitment practices and training that can support newcomers.UNHCR has said that including refugees in local economies can benefit both employers and host communities. Refugees can fill labour gaps and contribute to economic growth, while businesses gain access to workers with varied skills and experience. The partnership aims to help make those connections more routine.Tent’s role is to bring companies together and help them act. A network of hundreds of employers offers a broader route to work than relying on individual businesses to develop programmes alone. It also gives companies a place to share approaches and learn from one another.Work as a first stepUlukaya has described a job as one of the most important milestones for refugees rebuilding their lives. That belief comes from the experience of hiring newcomers at Chobani, where language support and transportation helped people reach the workplace and contribute.A job does not resolve every difficulty faced by a displaced person. Refugees may still need housing, education, legal support and help reconnecting with family. But employment can provide income, routine and a sense of participation in the community. It can also give employers an opportunity to recognise the skills people bring with them.From his own arrival in the US in 1994 to the growth of Chobani and the launch of Tent, Ulukaya’s story has been shaped by the relationship between work and belonging. He began as a newcomer with no English and no personal network. He later built a company that hired hundreds of refugees and created a platform encouraging other businesses to do the same.Tent’s 400-plus-company network cannot guarantee a job for every refugee seeking one. It can, however, help employers identify barriers and create more routes into work. For Ulukaya, the aim is to make sure that arriving in a new country does not mean being shut out of the chance to contribute and build a future.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: 'Burn the boats': UCLA coach's fiery pregame speech before Oregon game was pure Hollywood
articles.summary: Bob Chesney's viral "burn the boats" tunnel speech fired up UCLA football before the Bruins dominated time of possession to beat Oregon at Autzen Stadium.
articles.body: It's official –– UCLA head coach Bob Chesney is straight out of Hollywood central casting and ready to be a certified star in college football. On Saturday, before the Bruins faced Oregon in Eugene, Chesney had his team take a knee in the Autzen Stadium tunnel for one final message. As his undefeated Bruins listened intently, Chesney turned into Tony D'Amato (Al Pacino) in Any Given Sunday. In the 1999 movie, D'Amato reminded his players, "We're in hell right now, gentlemen. Believe me. And, we can stay here, get the s–t kicked out of us, or we can fight our way back into the light. We can climb outta hell... one inch at a time." Chesney gave his boys a speech in a similar vein. The 49-year-old Hollywood newcomer chose to paraphrase Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés after his 1519 landing in Mexico with 600 troops. "They're about to go in and start the war, and he wants to make sure that nobody has any other thought," Chesney told Bruins. "No other thought than we're 100% positive we're winning this f–king battle. He looks around at the boats they'd have to go home on and says, 'Burn the f–king boats.' NICK SABAN TELLS THEO VON HIS FAMOUS SIDELINE INTENSITY WAS A CALCULATED STRATEGY, NOT EMOTION "There is no way out. We can't go that way (Chesney points to the sunlight outside Autzen Stadium). You gotta go through these motherf–kers." The Bruins stand up, chant something, and Chesney turns towards the tunnel. Like Tom Cruise about to strap in and go shoot down multiple Sukhoi Su-57 stealth fighters, Chesney grabs his sunglasses, locks them into place, seems to hit play on an Apple iWatch workout and walks down the ramp into battle. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE Chesney isn't the first inspirational speaker to use the "burn the boats" speech, but in the modern Internet era, he's the first to do it with such cinematic flair. The hair is perfect. The all-black shoes, pants and shirt and then the black sunglasses project something that none of us can remember from UCLA – hardness. After his burn the boats speech, the Bruins went out and dominated the time of possession – 39:15 to 20:45 – and beat Oregon 17-15. It was the first time they'd beaten Oregon on the road since 2004. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Was it a beautiful win? Not at all. Chesney was the first to admit it before his team boarded a plane back to Los Angeles, instead of a boat. Remember, they burned the boats. "So, if you're going to ask about complacency, you don't have to, because obviously there's enough on that film that we got to do a whole lot better if we want to win this next game and any to follow. We can't turn the ball over," Chesney told the media. "We can't get a field goal blocked. We can't do a lot of the things we did, letting the ball get down at the one-yard line, and all the other things that showed up in that game. There were moments where it really could have gone the other way, but I was really, really proud of the effort. Really, really proud of how hard they played. "Really, really proud of them being able to self-regulate in a hostile environment like that. Not an easy place to play, but I thought they did a really good job of it, and I'm proud of that effort." SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER There's bad news for the Bruins. Quarterback Nico Iamaleava is believed to be out for the season with a knee injury suffered Saturday. Where does Chesney go with the speeches from here? Will he channel Band of Brothers? Stay tuned. We're about to witness some of this guy's best work with a dream season in the works.

articles.body: Former The Real Housewives of Potomac star Mia Thornton is facing a felony theft-by-taking charge in Georgia over allegations that she removed furniture and a television worth thousands of dollars from a furnished Atlanta condo in October 2025. Receipts submitted to investigators placed the estimated value of the missing items at approximately $11,000, according to local reports at the time.The allegations concern the removal of the items in October 2025, several weeks before Thornton’s airport arrest. The charge remains unresolved, and the allegations have not been established in court.Details of Thornton’s airport arrestThornton was arrested in November 2025 at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport after officers responding to a wanted-person call at the Customs and Border Protection office discovered an active larceny warrant, Atlanta police said. She was taken into custody without incident.A judge subsequently set her bond at $2,500. articles.summary: When South African technology billionaire Koos Bekker bought Hadspen House and 16 acres of land in Somerset in 2013, the purchase marked the beginning of
articles.body: When South African technology billionaire Koos Bekker bought Hadspen House and 16 acres of land in Somerset in 2013, the purchase marked the beginning of a much larger project. The estate, now known as The Newt in Somerset, has grown to cover more than 2,700 acres through land purchases made by Bekker’s company, according to The Guardian. The business has developed into a luxury hotel and visitor attraction, with gardens, farmland, orchards, restaurants and shops. It says it employs more than 650 people who live in or come from the local area. For some residents, the estate has brought jobs and investment. Others are uneasy about its growing reach, raising questions about land ownership, local identity and how much influence one company should have in a rural community.From manor house to destinationHadspen House is a 17th-century country house near the towns of Bruton and Castle Cary. Bekker and his wife, Karen Roos, bought the property in 2013 and began developing it as a hospitality and horticultural destination. The Newt opened to visitors in 2019, built around the historic house and its gardens.The estate presents itself as a working countryside property, with gardens, woodland, farmland and cider orchards alongside a hotel, restaurants and visitor experiences. Its community page describes an operation that aims to connect hospitality with local food, landscape and heritage.The scale has changed considerably since those early plans. The Guardian reports that the company now controls more than 2,700 acres in the surrounding area, acquired through purchases made over the years. That landholding has helped shape The Newt’s growth, but it has also altered how some residents view the project.Jobs and local linksThe Newt says it employs more than 650 people who are either from or live within the local area. That is a substantial workforce for a rural business, and the company presents employment as a central part of its relationship with the community.The estate’s activities extend beyond hotel accommodation. Its gardens, farm, orchards, food businesses and visitor services require staff with a wide range of skills, from horticulture and food production to hospitality and retail. The Newt also says it works with local organisations and maintains relationships with community groups.For supporters, the growth has brought jobs, visitor spending and a new profile for the area. A major attraction can draw people who might otherwise pass through, supporting businesses and increasing demand for local services. The company’s employment figure is an important part of its case that the expansion has delivered tangible benefits.Yet jobs do not answer every concern. Some residents have questioned whether the growth of a single owner’s businesses and landholdings is changing the balance of local life. The debate is not only about whether The Newt creates employment, but also about who benefits from development and how decisions affect the people who already live nearby.Concerns about expansionAccording to The Guardian, local concerns range across the scale of the estate’s expansion, the use of pesticides and the commercial branding of nearby places. Residents have also raised issues such as flooding and the potential impact of the estate’s activities on the surrounding area.One point of contention has been the growing presence of The Newt’s name in local life. The newspaper reported that a nearby train station was renamed to include the hotel’s branding, a move criticised by some as an example of the company’s influence extending beyond its land.Other residents have objected to the acquisition of businesses and properties in nearby towns. The Newt’s reach into shops, pubs and other local enterprises has led some people to worry that a once-independent community could become increasingly identified with one private estate.These concerns do not necessarily mean that everyone opposes the project. The Newt’s supporters point to jobs and investment, while critics question whether the costs of expansion are being adequately considered. The disagreement reflects a wider challenge facing rural areas when a large private enterprise becomes a dominant local presence.What the company saysThe Newt’s official community page says that the estate is a part of the local area, rather than as a closed resort. It says the company values relationships with local organisations and highlights its workforce as evidence of its connection to Somerset.That account sits alongside the concerns reported by The Guardian. The two perspectives show the different ways residents and the company assess the estate’s role. The business emphasises employment, community links and the care of historic landscapes, while critics focus on the cumulative influence of land purchases and commercial activity.The estate’s community message also reflects a broader model of luxury tourism. It presents gardens, food and the countryside as part of the visitor experience, while relying on local workers and suppliers to operate the business. The approach may bring economic activity, but it can also raise questions about access, affordability and how a rural place is represented.A changing corner of SomersetThe Newt’s expansion has transformed a country house and its grounds into a large, multi-part operation. Its footprint now stretches across thousands of acres, while its businesses extend into hospitality, food, retail and visitor experiences.For residents, the changes are personal as well as economic. A new employer can offer valuable work, but rapid expansion may also affect housing, traffic, local businesses and the character of nearby towns. Those effects are not always experienced equally, which helps explain why the project has attracted both support and criticism.The debate around The Newt is ultimately about more than one hotel or garden. It asks how a community can welcome investment while retaining a voice in decisions that shape its future. The company says it employs hundreds of local people and works with community organisations. Residents who question its growth want to know how that influence will be balanced with local needs.Since Bekker bought Hadspen House and 16 acres in 2013, the project has grown into an estate controlling more than 2,700 acres nearby. Its workforce and visitor economy have made it an important part of the region, but its expansion has also prompted difficult questions. In Somerset, the future of The Newt is being debated not only as a business story, but as a test of how growth, community and local identity can coexist.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2010, a California man paid $2 for three old photographs at a junk shop; five years later, experts said one showed Billy the Kid playing croquet and had it insured for $5 million
articles.summary: Randy Guijarro of Fremont, California, paid $2 for an old photograph at an antique shop in 2010.
articles.body: Randy Guijarro of Fremont, California, paid $2 for an old photograph at an antique shop in 2010. The seemingly ordinary pictures turned out to include one of the most valuable images of the Old West, with an insurance value of $5 million.In 2010, Guijarro purchased the photograph for $2. He kept the 4-by-5-inch photograph, and at some point, he began to suspect it showed someone famous. So, he approached Kagin’s Inc., a company that deals in Western history and rare coins. Guijarro believed the picture was genuine, and he spent the next year working with experts to test that belief.Kagin’s said the photo shows Billy the Kid and members of the Lincoln County Regulators playing croquet. Friends, family and lovers were there, too. It shows the gang "playing a leisurely game of croquet alongside friends, family and lovers in the late summer of 1878”, the company said.Billy the Kid is one of the most notorious outlaws in American history. He was part of the Regulators and took part in the Lincoln County War in New Mexico. Legend has it that he killed between eight and 22 people. The company says the photo has been appraised and insured for $5 million and, if confirmed as authentic, would be only the second known image of him. The other is a tintype taken in New Mexico in 1880. A collector named William Koch bought it for $2.3 million in 2010.“When we first saw the photograph, we were understandably sceptical. An original Billy the Kid photo is the Holy Grail of Western Americana. We had to be certain that we could answer and verify where, when, how and why this photograph was taken,” Kagin’s senior numismatist David McCarthy told the LA Times.But Kagin’s still had one question: where was the photo taken? McCarthy flew to New Mexico to find the exact location. He called the moment an ‘incredible thrill’. “We have these moments of discovery every once in a while. You get goosebumps,” he told ABC News.For McCarthy, it was the posture and face that stood out. "The way he held his body in the photo, [a] sort of confident slouch. [He's] facing the camera, dead on, with a grin on his face," McCarthy told the outlet. His team found that the building was about a 15-minute walk from the home of John Tunstall, the Englishman who mentored Billy the Kid. Tunstall, McCarthy said, wrote in his diary about playing croquet with friends. Research also suggested that a wedding or a cattle drive after the war was the likely reason for the gathering, he said."Billy the Kid is incredibly famous. [But] he wasn't shooting people all the time. He had friends he cared about. He had women he chased. It (the photograph) opens up the idea of the humanity of a character like Billy the Kid,” McCarthy said.Kagin noted that this picture was more special than the first, as it revealed ‘a slice of life’.A documentary on the National Geographic Channel also tells the story of how the photo was found and authenticated. “This is such a great story. He's one of the great outlaws and personalities,” Kagin added.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: King Charles and Queen Camilla’s royal beehives produce hundreds of jars of honey; the Queen’s own honey is sold to raise money for charity
articles.summary: King Charles III and Queen Camilla’s royal beekeeping activities are linking honey production with charitable fundraising and wider biodiversity efforts.
articles.body: King Charles III and Queen Camilla’s royal beekeeping activities are linking honey production with charitable fundraising and wider biodiversity efforts. Buckingham Palace and Clarence House house six beehives between them, producing honey for use in royal kitchens, while Queen Camilla’s own honey, produced at her home in Wiltshire, is sold through Fortnum & Mason to raise money for charity. According to the Royal Family’s official website, she also supports Bees for Development, which works to reduce poverty and improve biodiversity in more than 50 countries. Bee-friendly flowers planted at Balmoral and Highgrove further support efforts to encourage wild bees and other pollinators across royal gardens.How do King Charles and Queen Camilla’s royal bees produce honeyBuckingham Palace is home to four beehives situated on an island in the middle of the garden lake, while Clarence House has two hives in its garden. The bees forage on the nectar plants growing on the island and throughout the gardens. The website reports that the colonies produce enough honey during the season for Buckingham Palace and Clarence House to be self-sufficient, with more than 300 jars produced in the previous year for use in the Palace kitchens.The honey is used by royal chefs throughout the year, including for guests attending official events, garden parties and receptions. The Royal Family website states that Buckingham Palace honey is often incorporated into honey madeleines, used as a filling for chocolate truffles or served in honey and cream sponge. The two Clarence House hives are home to more than 90,000 bees and produce around 40 pounds of honey annually, according to the same source. These details illustrate the role of beekeeping within the royal household, where honey is both a food ingredient and a product of the gardens maintained at royal residences.How does Queen Camilla’s honey support charitable causesQueen Camilla also produces honey at her home in Wiltshire, which is sold through Fortnum & Mason to raise money for charitable causes. The Royal Family's website identifies Mirabel, Nigeria's first Sexual Assault Referral Centre, as a beneficiary of funds raised through the honey. Queen Camilla became Patron of Mirabel in 2021, when she was the Duchess of Cornwall. The charitable proceeds from her honey production therefore connect her personal interest in beekeeping with support for an organisation providing a specialist service in Nigeria.Her involvement in beekeeping also extends to Bees for Development, where she became president in 2020 while serving as Duchess of Cornwall. articles.title: Drunk civic police approaches Didi with knife, FIR registered
articles.summary: Knife-wielding civic volunteer detained after approaching Mamata Banerjee near Kalighat home; FIR filed, police probe underway with CCTV review.
articles.body: Kolkata: A drunk civic volunteer, armed with a knife, came within a few metres of former chief minister Mamata Banerjee as she stepped out of her Kalighat home on Tuesday to inaugurate a Durga Puja, the first by her this season. After an FIR was lodged, Kalighat police detained Tannishtha Saha for questioning. Banerjee is a Z-plus protectee.In her police complaint, Rajya Sabha MP Dola Sen said that around 6 pm, Saha “reportedly known as civic volunteer and a drug addict” approached Banerjee violently and tried to attack her with a knife and claimed to be her niece. She hurled abuses at Banerjee and even lay down on the road, the complaint said.Kolkata Police did not issue a formal statement but a senior officer at Lalbazar said they are in the process of launching an investigation. “We are trying to fix the sequence of events. The accused has been detained and an FIR is being drawn up. We are speaking to eyewitnesses, including those in her security. We have also collected CCTV footage from the area,” he said.Banerjee was heading to the Kalighat Milan Sangha pandal near her residence to inaugurate the puja. Several others were walking along with her when the alleged attempted attack took place. The former CM remained unfazed after the incident and walked down to the pandal, where she summoned a child to cut the ribbon. She offered prayers and was seen chatting with the locals.“Such an attack on a former CM who enjoys Z+ security right outside her residence is unprecedented. An independent probe must be carried out to ascertain if this was pre-planned,” said former KMC MMiC Baiswanor Chattopadhyay, adding that this was the second attack on Banerjee after the one in Halisahar, where her vehicle was vandalised on Aug 9.Trinamool national spokesperson Saket Gokhale said, “A drug addict reached Mamata Banerjee’s residence today and tried to attack her with a knife. articles.title: DAVID MARCUS: On the ground in Middle America, four issues will decide the senate, and none are affordability
articles.summary: Fraud in Minnesota, growth in Ohio, and culture in Texas are driving 2026 midterm election races more than affordability, ground reporting reveals.
articles.body: For nearly a year now, the assumption from the chattering classes has been that the 2026 midterm election will be decided on the issue of affordability, but on the ground, in the mid-American states that will decide control of the senate, it is local issues that dominate, not the vague, overarching question of prices. Part of the problem with nationalizing the affordability issue is that it originated in New York City with the campaign of current socialist mayor Zohran Mamdani. But Gotham is a unique case that is always very expensive. The last time Manhattan was affordable was when the Dutch bought it from the Indians. In the middle of the country, including Michigan, Ohio, Minnesota, and Texas, all of which this column has visited in the past month, the economy is a major issue, as polls indicate, but it is not the same existential crisis that it was for voters we spoke with in 2022 or 2024. DAVID MARCUS: IN SPRINGFIELD, OHIO, ONLY TRUMP CAN MEND MAGA-CHAMBER OF COMMERCE RIFT I met Reggie at a restaurant in Springfield, Ohio. He’s recently married, reading self-help books, and in construction, he told Fox News Digital, "There’s work, wages are good, that’s not an issue, prices are prices, and gas has gone down with the tax holiday." Reggie was referring to Ohio’s decision to temporarily suspend gas tax, resulting in a price under four dollars in the Buckeye State. DAVID MARCUS: IN DAYTON, OHIO, BOTH PARTIES FACE BITTER POLITICAL DESPONDENCY In fact, in no state this column visited did it seem as if cost of living was the prime driver of the electorate. So what is it? Let’s take it state by state. Minnesota: Fraud The cleanest and clearest way to know what issue is driving any community of voters is when they bring something up before you do, and in Minnesota, almost everyone I spoke with brought up fraud with no coaxing. DAVID MARCUS: PEGGY FLANAGAN'S DEI RECORD AND FRAUD SCANDAL PUT MINNESOTA SENATE RACE IN THE SPOTLIGHT Over the past year, the scope and scale of fraud in Minnesota’s Somali community has come to shocking light and it is something that Democratic Lt. Gov. and Senate candidate Peggy Flanagan cannot escape, and that her GOP challenger, Michelle Tafoya is rightfully milking like a top-prize heifer at the Minnesota state fair. When it comes to the economy, Americans are not in fear, but they do have questions and doubts. This is a race that almost nobody expected to be competitive just a few months ago, but that is because pundits were reading the national mood, not the mood in Minnesota, which can only be found on the ground, and which is very angry. Ohio: Creating Growth Dayton, Ohio is full of absolutely lovely people, many of whom I spoke with, and I wish I could say kinder things about it, but it is an all but a dead city. Stunningly beautiful buildings sit abandoned, like coarse reminders of better days. What Daytonites, as well as Ohians in general, want and need is growth. It's not that they can’t afford their lives, it's that their communities do not thrive, do not grow, and they want to know if a once great state can be great again. THE BLUE WAVE LOOKS REAL UNTIL YOU LOOK A LITTLE CLOSER In the race between Republican incumbent Sen. John Husted and Democrat Sherrod Brown, the winner will be the one who can convince Ohio voters that they have a plan to bring cities like Dayton back. Michigan: Sustaining Growth Compared to Dayton, Ohio, Grand Rapids, Michigan seems like Oz. As my Uber driver told me on the drive in, "Everyone I take back to the airport raves about the city. You will, too." And here we are. Like Detroit, which this column also recently visited, Grand Rapids is a buzzing town, neat-necktied producers of wealth roam the streets discussing deals and going to lunch. You also see kids in a downtown that screams not just wealth, but authenticity. LIZ PEEK: TWO TROUBLED SENATE RACES COULD SPOIL DEMOCRATS' BLUE-WAVE FANTASY In the race between Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed for senate, the primary issue is who can sustain the growth that Michigan has experienced, and who gets the credit: Democrat Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, or President Donald Trump. Texas: Culture Texas is another state where the most pressing issue is not economic, but rather, in this case, cultural. Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton has universally been tagged as the worst candidate of 2026, and yet not only is he a successful attorney general, he is also undeniably Texan, for all his big faults. In James Talarico, Democrats have a once vegan, Unitarian-style Christian, who has admitted his biggest concern in life is making sure trans kids can get access to controversial surgical procedures. Now that Talerico is back from his two week bout of the flu, the cultural questions will be coming hot and heavy, and he has no good answer for them. EVERYONE IS WATCHING TEXAS AND MICHIGAN. AS A POLLSTER, I KNOW WHERE THE REAL STORY IS When it comes to the economy, Americans are not in fear, but they do have questions and doubts. When I was talking with Reggie in Springfield, Greg came in. He sells autonomous lawn mowers to golf courses and commercial parks. Eventually Reggie, who again, is in construction, asked a bit nervously, "How good are the autonomous forklifts getting?" CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Greg confirmed that the forklifts were getting very good, but added something interesting. "A landscaping company doesn’t make money off the guy on a mower," he said, adding, "They make money from the guy trimming and edging. Now that's two guys and you can do an extra job every day." I’m not sure Reggie was fully convinced or relieved. I’m not sure if I was for that matter, but this is the level of economic anxiety that exists in Middle America, not dread over whether food can be put on the table. articles.title: Massive fire destroys 400-year-old food market, leaving historic landmark in ruins
articles.summary: Flames tore through the Enfants Rouges market in Paris, destroying about 20 vendor stalls inside the historic market founded in 1615. It was the city's oldest covered food market.
articles.body: Marché des Enfants Rouges, the oldest covered food market in Paris, was engulfed in flames in the early hours of Monday, Oct. 12, destroying vendor stalls and a piece of local history. The fire broke out around 3 a.m. Monday, with firefighters working for several hours to quell the flames, Reuters reported. The fire left the market in ruins, with about 20 merchants losing their stalls, according to Ariel Weil, the mayor of central Paris. CELEBRITY CHEF LEAVES ONE ICONIC INGREDIENT OUT OF HER COOKING AND DINERS CAN'T TELL "Fire brought under control but market totally devastated. Avoid the area around Rue de Bretagne," Weil said in a post on X on Monday morning. "9 hoses, including 2 high-powered ones, were required to bring the disaster under control," Brigade des Sapeurs-Pompiers de Paris (BSPP), the city's primary fire and rescue service, said in a post on X. "150 firefighters were mobilized tonight," Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire posted on X. "I want to express my full gratitude to them." He added that an investigation is underway to determine the cause of the fire. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "We will find temporary locations for the businesses so that all their activities can be maintained," the post said. Located in the Marais district of Paris in the city's 3rd arrondissement, the market was founded in 1615 during the reign of King Louis XIII. A popular destination for both tourists and locals, the market drew people from all over the world, according to the website for the city of Paris. The name translates directly to "Market of the Red Children," a moniker that came from a nearby orphanage, the Hospice des Enfants Rouges, where the children usually wore red, according to the city's website. Before its destruction, the market housed restaurants where people could sit down for a meal or a cocktail. articles.title: Formula 1 Is Finally Returning to Africa With Major Grand Prix Announcement!
articles.summary: Formula 1 fans have been waiting more than three decades for the sport to return to Africa, and that wait is finally coming to an end. F1 officially announce...
articles.body:
Formula 1 fans have been waiting more than three decades for the sport to return to Africa, and that wait is finally coming to an end. F1 officially announced Tuesday that Rwanda will host the African Grand Prix under a new 10 year agreement, marking a historic moment for the sport. The race is expected to join the calendar in the early 2030s.

The new Grand Prix will take place at a purpose-built circuit planned for Bugesera, approximately 25 miles south of Rwanda's capital, Kigali.

The track will be designed to meet FIA Grade 1 standards, the level required to host Formula 1 races. Former F1 driver Alex Wurz and renowned circuit designer Hermann Tilke are involved in developing the plans, with the layout expected to take advantage of the area's natural elevation changes.

The venue will be part of a larger development project intended to boost tourism, attract international investment and create new opportunities for businesses and local communities.

However, construction still needs to be completed before the race can take place. F1 has not yet announced an exact date for the inaugural event.

A Return More Than 30 Years in the Making

The announcement ends a long absence for Formula 1 in Africa. The championship last raced on the continent in 1993, when the South African Grand Prix was held at the historic Kyalami circuit.

Since then, there have been repeated efforts to bring F1 back, with South Africa also exploring a potential return. Rwanda's agreement now gives the sport a confirmed long-term plan for racing on the continent again.

The move is particularly significant for seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton, who has repeatedly spoken about his desire to see Formula 1 return to Africa.

The African Grand Prix could open the door to a new generation of fans and help expand the sport's global reach.

Rwanda's deal represents more than another destination on the calendar. It gives Formula 1 an opportunity to connect with a growing audience while bringing international attention and investment to the region.

There are still major steps ahead before the first race becomes reality, but the agreement is official.

After years of speculation, Formula 1 is finally heading back to Africa, and the sport's next chapter could begin in Rwanda in the early 2030s.
